en: Uncle Bakai, I shall care for him twelve years!
If he becomes a hero like his father,
Uncle Bakai, leopard,
Let me return and see Talas.
If he fails to take after his father,
Uncle Bakai, hear my words!
Let me die before my appointed death!
The hoof left by the winged steed,
The little one, a full-blooded warhorse—
Round his neck I shall tie an amulet.
Until his age reaches twelve,
I shall care for him with aching love.
King Bakai, my uncle,
Before you, the child
I shall place as your protection,
The only one left by the hero.
Royal uncle, my sultan,
I shall give him to you as your support!
I, the widow left by Manas,
Showing my fierce resolve,
The little orphan, grown upright,
I shall raise to manhood as a hero,
Make him equal to the sons of warriors,
Uncle Bakai, my sultan,
And put him into your hands.
Make him know what he does not know;
Show knowledge to the orphan.
The blaze-headed horses on the hills,
Do not turn them out to graze upon the hills.
Your friend gone to the other world—
Never let his absence be felt!
When the khan dies, the old man
Would settle along the valley.
Do not walk into that gathering.
‘That aged beard,’ they would say,
And he would gain an ill name.
Keeping away from throngs and assemblies,
Uncle Bakai, keep tending the camels in your grief.
Until I come from Bukhara,
Until my prince sees you,
May he not die in misery,
May death not come to him untimely.
The black riding camel with the broad hump,
Jelmaiyan, left by my khan Manas—
Uncle Bakai, bearer of good fortune,
Submit to what I say.
When he returns to Talas,
‘From your gray-maned father Manas
It was left in trust,’ tell him.
‘Sacrifice it in your father's name,’ tell him.
There is a golden halter upon its head.
‘Your wretched mother Kanykei—
Take it to her,’ tell him.
Uncle Bakai, my sultan,
Submit to what I say.
Among the camels, Jelmaiyan—
Give it to your orphan Semetey.
Uncle Bakai, leopard,
Though an animal, it is my heirloom.
Jelmaiyan, left by Manas,
Was a sacred beast itself.
Except that it was an animal,
It was wiser than a human.
When your friend Manas died,
Hunching like a quail,
Jelmaiyan crouched down.
In the valley where the king departed,
Jelmaiyan knelt down.
Lamenting and sobbing like a human,
Gathering tears in its eyes,
Jelmaiyan shed them.
Fifteen days, fifteen nights,
Day and night for all those days,
Keeping mourning, without grazing,
Jelmaiyan remained kneeling.
God had taken its lord.
Among the camels, Jelmaiyan
Had become an omen.
Until Semetey returns,
Until your orphan sees the camel,
Its neck toward the other camels
Jelmaiyan will not turn.
Even if you strike it with a stick,
Jelmaiyan will not rise at all.
Facing the direction of prayer,
Jelmaiyan will kneel down.
Gathering tears in its eyes,
Jelmaiyan will shed them.
When Jelmaiyan stands thus,
The birch will weep, the willow will weep.
‘My blood-shedding Manas, do not die,’
Old Bakai will weep in grief.
‘When his beast is like this,
How can his people restrain themselves?’ they will say;
Every soul who sees it will weep.
Gray-maned uncle, King Bakai,
Plucking feather grass to feed it,
Giving it water from a leather pail,
You will endure great hardship.
Until your orphan returns,
The black riding camel with the broad hump,
Jelmaiyan, you must tend.
If your foal Semetey appears safe and sound,
Sacrifice it in your friend Manas's name.
There is a golden halter upon its head.
‘Take it to poor Kanykei,’ say,
And entrust it to my orphan.
When the six villains plundered the precious goods,
When they stirred up fierce trouble,
I was ruined and gained an ill name.
The six keen blades fallen from heaven,
A surpassing treasure for whoever held them,
When drawn from their sheaths with a shout,
Would not return without drinking blood.
When swung, they did not shrink from stone;
When wielded, they did not recoil from iron.
Through the misfortune of your bitch Kanykei,
They remained behind, uncle,
My dark eyes blinded with grief,
In the hands of those six villains.
That treasure was worth the whole world,
From the famed gray-maned Manas
Those keen blades remained as gifts.
One does not err in saying it:
For your friend Manas expressly,
Those keen blades fell from heaven.
The edge of the sword,
Zulpukor, held by Khan Manas,
My royal uncle, King Bakai's Joikuma,
Ajybai's Achalbars,
Almambet's Joikuma,
The hero Chubak's Kylbolot,
The sword with a bent tip—
Arkesken, held by the hero Syrgak:
Those were the six mighty blades,
That treasure left by the precious one gone to the other world.
Uncle Bakai, you were not there.
When they found his countless herds,
The six foolish-born slaves,
When they slashed my breast open,
As I lost consciousness and staggered,
As I lay unable to regain my senses,
The six slaves beat me tirelessly.
When they dragged me like a carcass in kok-boru,
When they plundered my treasure,
When they plunged me into a dark night,
The six keen blades fell
Into the hands of the slave Kobosh.
If my orphan comes to your side,
Uncle Bakai, leopard,
Submit to what I say.
‘They remained from his father,’ say,
And with noble, gracious words,
Recover them for your orphan Semetey.
Uncle Bakai, dear friend,
However I lament, your friend will not be found.
Hungry, we fled to Bukhara.
My open wound will not close.
The place I am going is broad Bukhara.
There are hoe-working Tajiks and Sarts;
Those who never had their fill when asking to eat,
Who never gave up their greed—
Now, uncle Bakai, consider:
The lordly Kyrgyz will not be found there.
Where the cuckoo sang in the willow,
Where the nightingale spoke in the garden,
Where we moved uphill to summer among tamarisks,
With thoroughbreds and noble steeds together
Tethered along the horse-line—
Where is Talas, the land we inhabited?
When your orphan goes to Bukhara
And joins the ranks of its people,
When will the day come to see Talas again?
If my wretched life does not die in suffering,
Where is a people like my Kyrgyz?
Its chervil is thick as a wrist;
When you look at its deer,
They are like pale, blaze-faced cows.
Where is a land like my Talas?
Exhausted, I fled toward Bukhara.
Uncle Bakai, my gray-maned hero,
When will the day come to return to Talas?
Its leaves are like hides,
Its black worms as big as thumbs;
Its mountains have snow,
Its forests have rooks.
Its otters crawl upon the sand;
Wild ewes and rams gather,
And young horses are raced in play.
Of merry games and laughter,
Brave men never had their fill.
Where is a place like my Keng-Kol?
It was the homeland left by Sultan Manas.
When will the day come to see the Argyn again?
Far away, toward the khan's city,
I go crossing the heights, uncle!
I was a gorge; I have become a road.
When my leopard lord died,
Toward this Bukhara,
Fleeing, wandering, humiliated,
Without equipment, my strength gone,
I go, grown thin.
Toward my father Temir Khan's city,
Unable to gather my wits,
I go in misery.
May my gray-maned lord not die;
May a woman never know plunder!
Uncle Bakai, listen:
Giving the swan to be eaten by a bird of prey,
The orphan left by my companion,
If I go wretchedly to Bukhara,
I shall have him called the Sarts' son.
Giving the goose to be eaten by a bird of prey,
This Semetey left by my khan,
The only child left by the blood-shedder,
I shall have him called another man's son.
Uncle, the provisions you have just given
Have given us strength for six months.
What I shall sip for thirst from time to time,
Uncle Bakai, is six skins of milk.
When you came enduring hardship,
The wether you gave as a gift—
Until death, the heart will not forget
The deeds of the six villains in Talas.
When I was exhausted and weary,
You followed and pursued me,
Caught up with me in this place,
And set it aside as provisions—
The wether gray-maned Bakai gave.
Drawing their bows like rain,
Firing their arrows like hail,
Until death, the heart will not forget
The deeds of the forty companions in Talas.
The great dogs joined together,
Uncle Bakai, gray-maned hero,
And broke up my camp in Keng-Kol.
The child bestowed by fate is young;
Against those raving dogs
I left without taking my revenge!
They scattered my people from Talas;
The child written into my fortune is young.
None heeded another's words;
None could bear the sight of another.
The plundering dogs acted on their own.
Leaving my possessions to them,
My poor self escaped in flight!
He broke into my treasure and took it.
The child I took as my support is young.
Uncle Bakai, I was left weeping in grief.
Above my looming dark head,
When I wept, no one saw my tears.
Parted from my possessions,
Though I lamented, God did not take me.
This orphan I cradle,
When he reaches twelve,
If I see Talas, I shall have no regret.
